content.text: Merged and captured. Now the last merge step — the production verification this change genuinely needs.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/verify-in-production

# Verify in production

A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
unattended: an automatic check, end to end, that the run can make from this repository.
Where it cannot, the answer is almost always to file nothing and say the change is
unverified; asking a person is a rare exception, and no automatic check existing is not
on its own enough to earn one.

## When it fires: after the merge, never before

**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.

The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:

- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists.
- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.

So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.

## First: does this file anything at all?

Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:

1. **Can you watch it work in this session — now, or after a wait you can sit through?**
   Then do that and file nothing — the bar is "could you", not "did you already". If it
   becomes readable inside the session you are in, waiting for it is cheaper than every
   mechanism below. (2)
2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
   that comes back.
3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
   its rules — that is what you file.

The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.
And the test above only files point assertions: when the merge completes a **larger element** —
one that earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue — the ~week-later review of how the
whole design fared is [production-retrospective](../production-retrospective/SKILL.md)'s
separate call, made beside this one.

## Second: which runner can read it? If neither, file nothing

There are two runners, and the artifact's address decides which one a verification
gets — never preference:

- **A public URL** — a Pages site, a deployed config, a published module, a live
  `/version.json` — files the **coded form**: declarative probes an agentless queue
  task (`claudinite-tasks/verify-production`) fetches and judges Action-side, where
  egress exists. No session ever runs, so there is no egress wall to hit — this is
  the lane for exactly the class that used to park.
- **A GitHub read** — an issue's state, a file at HEAD, a workflow run's conclusion —
  files the **agentic form**: an unattended session on this repository, whose reach
  is narrower than yours — **GitHub, through its own tools, in the repositories its
  routine's scope names** — and nothing else. Take the read you are about to write
  into `Verify:` and answer, in one sentence, *which tool call the run makes, in
  which repository*. **Another repo is the standard trap**, because the read looks
  ordinary and the wall is invisible from here — a `Verify:` naming a member repo
  parks minutes after being picked, on a scope denial. (4)
  A cross-repo artifact with a
  public URL — a member's stamp on `raw.githubusercontent.com`, its Pages site — is
  not walled at all: it is a URL, and the coded form reads it.
- **Neither** — a login-walled console, a private dashboard, a repository outside
  scope with no public surface — **file nothing**: say in your reply that the change
  is unverified and what would prove it. That is a filter, not a fork: an unreadable
  artifact is a reason not to file. Filing anyway spends a session rediscovering the
  wall and then parks `needs-human-action`, which is the human's-memory outcome this
  skill exists to avoid.

Where the subject is the **fleet** rather than this repo — every member's stamp, every
member's CI — this queue is the wrong runner for it whatever you file. It belongs to a
routine that holds fleet scope, if the project has one, and to nobody otherwise.

**Asking a person is the rare exception**, not the fallback. The bar is not "no
automatic check exists" — most changes clear that and still get nothing. It is that a
silent failure here would be **costly**, and you would be willing to interrupt the
person today to have them look. If you would not, the change goes unverified and you say
so. When it does clear that bar, file an ordinary issue — never a queue item: title it
the same `Verify in production: …`, carry `Original-issue:` and attach it as that
issue's sub-issue, and write the body per
[writing-handover-issues](../writing-handover-issues/SKILL.md) — somebody else runs it,
so the checklist is the artifact. **No mark, no
`Not-before:`, no `Retry-every:`, no `Model:`**: nothing in it is the queue's, and a mark
would buy only a session that parks. Assign it to whoever owns the release, and say in
your reply that you are spending their attention and why it was worth it.

## What you file

**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. **Every field a run reads is one
block on the first lines of the description**, ahead of your prose — the same placement
[`/do-later`](../do-later/SKILL.md) files under, and what gives the retry below one place to
rewrite `Not-before:`. Then say what changed and why it could not be watched now.

### The coded form — for a URL-readable artifact

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
Task: claudinite-tasks/verify-production
Live-probe: <url> :: <assertion that becomes true when the release lands>
Verify-probe: <url> :: <the assertion being verified>
Retry-every: <how often to re-probe while not yet live, e.g. 6 hours>
```

The probes are the whole check, executed in code by the task the `Task:` line names —
no session, no `Model:`. `Live-probe:` is `In-production-when:` made executable and
`Verify-probe:` is `Verify:`; both classes are required, repeat either line for more
probes, and the assertion grammar (`status`, `contains`, `matches`, the `json` value
ops) is documented at its one home,
[`probes.mjs`](../../../claudinite-tasks/tasks/verify-production/probes.mjs). A
liveness probe failing re-arms the item by `Retry-every:`; a verify probe failing
against a live release reopens `Original-issue:` with what was asserted and what was
read; all passing closes the item with that evidence. No `Not-before:` is needed: a
coded run costs seconds, so probing from the moment of filing is the point, not a
waste — see the watch-it-fail step below.

### The agentic form — for a GitHub read

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
Model: sonnet
```

In either form, no `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has
already closed and there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.

- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait.
  "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.basics` at 60906.12 or
  higher." "Any session started after this
  landed — check the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge
  is not a production condition, neither is elapsed time, and neither is anything the run
  cannot read.
- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read the run can
  actually make (the gate above): a file's content, an issue's state, a run's conclusion.
  "Issue #100 on that repo is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check
  the sweep works". A `Verify:` naming a person's step does not belong in this form at all —
  that is the rare human step above, an ordinary issue that never carries the mark.
- **`Not-before:`** is the queue's own wait field: adoption holds the run until the moment has
  passed. Aim it just past the release you expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
  yet live, it re-arms `Not-before:` to **now + `Retry-every:`** — never the old value plus it.
  Size it to the release you wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in
  minutes.

Then the mark, as `/do-later` applies it: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**, the one label the scheduler
run adopts — both forms alike. The agentic form's `Model: sonnet` is in its block because that
is the work: reading a live artifact and judging an assertion against it; the coded form names
no model, because nothing runs but code. Never `Automerge:` — a verification has nothing to
merge. If the mark doesn't exist in the repo yet, say so and leave the issue — it appears on the
next scheduler run.

## Tell the agentic run how to converge

The coded form needs none of this: its verdicts — requeue, pass, reopen — are the machinery's,
so its body ends with your prose and the playbook below would only be read as instructions by
something that takes none.

For the agentic form, end the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole
brief, and the run decides nothing: it executes this playbook.

**The transition off this issue is `converge-item.mjs`** — the command your instructions'
converge step names — **and never your own hand.** It reaches no network and needs none: it
reads the item you hand it, plans every side effect, and prints the calls for your own GitHub
tools to make. A session with no route to `api.github.com` runs it exactly like any other;
that is what it is for, so there is nothing here to improvise. **Never write a
`task:status:*` label by hand**: a hand-set `task:status:done` on an issue left open is a pass
recorded nowhere the queue reads, and the done label then hides the item from the leash, so
nothing ever comes back for it. (5)
If the command refuses, it is telling you this item is not yours to converge — say so and stop.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
   run, or elapsed time. If it turns out you cannot read it at all from here, that is
   `--outcome action`, naming the read and who can make it — not a silent walk-away.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: converge `--outcome done`, its `--summary` carrying the
   evidence actually read (the version, the value, the path); the command closes this issue.
   Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened
   instead and where you read it, then converge `--outcome done`, its summary linking that
   comment — the verification did its job by finding the fault, and the fault is now that
   issue's.
3. **Not yet live** → the one branch that converges nothing, because the run is not over: set
   `Not-before:` to **now + `Retry-every:`** — the instant you are
   reading this at, never the old value the field carries — **clear the issue's
   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

   Measure from the instant you read, because the queue releases a sleeping item on the
   first hourly pass past its moment, so by the time a run reads the field it is already
   behind — old + `Retry-every: 1 day` lands in the past again, the item goes ready on the
   very next pass, and a daily retry spends a session an hour. (6)

## Then watch it fail, and say what you filed

A coded verification runs for seconds, so its first execution is not left to faith: dispatch
the scheduler workflow (its `workflow_dispatch`) and
watch the first run report **not yet live** — proof the probes execute and fail for the right
reason instead of passing vacuously;
the same item then flips on its own once the release lands. A first run that *passes* before
the release you expected deserves a hard look, because a probe that cannot fail proves
nothing. The agentic form sleeps until its `Not-before:` and has no cheap forced run; filing
it correctly is the watch.

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

Tools for listing GitHub Actions resources.
Use this tool to list workflows in a repository, or list workflow runs, jobs, and artifacts for a specific workflow or workflow run.

[{"number":2225,"title":"Let every entry point survive its own exit","body":"Replaces #2082, which is closed: its diff predated the `claudinite-tasks` `public/` → `src/` move, so 8 of its 51 conflicts were modify/delete against paths that no longer exist. This re-derives the same change against today's tree, which also picks up entry points added since.

## The premise, measured

An entry point's catch that calls `process.exit(1)` after printing discards whatever stdout has not drained. Node's stdout is synchronous for files and for pipes on Linux, so this does **not** show up in a small test — the 64 KB pipe buffer absorbs everything. It appears as soon as the reader applies backpressure:

| exit path | lines delivered | status |
|---|---|---|
| `process.exit(1)` | 309 of 200,000 | 1 |
| `process.exitCode = 1` | 200,000 of 200,000 | 1 |

Same exit status, all of the output. That is the whole change.

## Why it is safe here

All 27 sites are entry-point guards under `import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href`, and none waits on the event loop after the catch — so letting the process end naturally is equivalent to forcing it, minus the truncation.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 3809 pass, 0 fail.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — exit 0; remaining advisories are pre-existing kinds (`provenance-integrity`, `design-doc-status-banner`, `fixture-git-housekeeping`) in unrelated files.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` — exit 0.

## Not done here

Four task provenance files (`basics/ci-performance`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline`, `claudinite-growth/growth-dedup`, `claudinite-lifecycle/update`) are still empty, so the tool refuses a `policy-changed` entry on them — a first entry must be `born`. Writing `born` for tasks this change did not create would be false history, so they are left for the backfill. `provenance-change-recorded` is advisory until 2026-10-04 and reports them.

It does not close it — the converge does that, and the item is the marked issue itself.

## What changed

`frequency` was read at exactly one door, `normalizeTaskDeclaration`, as the cadence term it always meant. That door is gone. In its place the field is **rejected by name**, naming the term to write:

- `src/contract/task-contract.mjs` — the door and its `@legacy-tolerance advisory:legacy-task-fields retire:#1732` marker are deleted; `validateTaskDeclaration` reports `the task declares "frequency", which is retired` with the `due:<cadence>` to write (or `"trigger": "request"` for `manual`, which meant no schedule at all).
- `task.schema.json` — the deprecated property is deleted. The file is `additionalProperties: false`, so an editor now flags it too.
- `worldRules/legacy-task-fields.mjs` — the frequency branch goes: the advisory covers a door, and asking for an optional rename would understate a declaration that no longer runs. Its `why` and the module header drop the field; the trigger half is untouched.
- `worldRules/task-declaration-shape.mjs` — **blocking** where it used to advise, and it no longer treats the field as a statement of "when". The runtime rejects the declaration, so the author-time surface says the same thing; the two validate one contract, which is what stops them drifting.

`cadenceTermFor` **stays** in `calendar.mjs`: the `task-cadence-terms` migration record and its engine rewrite still spell the mapping, and a member converging after this still needs that rewrite.

The `trigger` derivation, its `retire:#1789` marker and the advisory's trigger branch are untouched, per the correction on #1732.

## Which reading I took

The brief says "delete … the shape check's acceptance". I read deleting the acceptance as *flagging the field blocking*, not as leaving the check silent on it — a silent check would let a member's `task.json` pass CI and then fail at load. That matches how the check already handles `precondition` and `precondition_signals`, and matches the contract module's own stated invariant that the two surfaces cannot drift.

## The diff reaches past `packs/claudinite-tasks` — deliberately, and `AUTOMERGE: no`

```
AUTOMERGE: no — engine-tests/task-declarations-to-json.test.mjs (modified test) is covered by no allow term;
packs/claudinite-dashboard/src/derive/model.mjs (modified code) is covered by no allow term;
packs/claudinite-dashboard/test/model.test.mjs (modified test) is covered by no allow term;
packs/claudinite-tasks/task.schema.json (modified code) is covered by no allow term
```

Two surfaces outside the pack held **their own copy of the door**, each pinned to the contract's by a drift guard. Both guards fired, which is what they exist for:

1. **`engine/migrations/task-declarations-to-json.mjs`'s codemod** (unchanged) was pinned against the contract's door. The door is gone, so its guard now pins against `cadenceTermFor` — the mapping the pack still spells, and the one the codemod's own comment already named.
2. **The dashboard's page-side door** read a cadence off `frequency` for another repo's declaration. After this change such a declaration does not run at all in the repo that owns it, so showing a cadence would promise a next anchor nothing reaches. The page now reads only the expression the declaration states; the shared vector set stays, with the retired field still among the shapes, so the two readings still cannot drift apart unseen.

The fourth path is inside the pack: `task.schema.json` is JSON, which matches none of `javascript-changes` / `test-changes` / `doc-changes`. The brief asked for the schema property's deletion, so the policy as written could not have passed even on the narrowest possible diff — worth noting when the next such policy is predicted.

The wide diff is the reviewable signal the brief asked for, not something to route around. The abstraction that would have kept it in one place: one door, read by both the page and the codemod, rather than three spellings of it held together by guards — the page cannot import the contract (`node:` builtins) and the engine imports no pack, so the duplication is structural today.

## Deliberately left out

- **No version bump and no `VERSIONS.md` row**, though the brief asked for both. `.github/workflows/pack-versions.yml` states it: *"every push to main cuts a new version for each pack whose shipping content moved … A pull request never bumps a pack itself."* The migration record carries the same note (#1726). `claudinite-tasks` and `claudinite-dashboard` both cut post-merge.

## Separate finding, filed rather than fixed here

#2139 — the `task-cadence-terms` migration record's `appliesTo` probes `packs/claudinite-tasks/calendar.mjs`, a path #1890 moved to `src/contract/calendar.mjs` on 2026-09-14. Both the mount and repo-root forms miss, so the record has read "not capable" — and stayed inert — since that day. That undercuts this retirement's premise for anyone who converged after it. Repointing it makes a codemod start writing to members' own files fleet-wide, so it gets its own review gate rather than riding a policy predicted from the door-removal diff.

## Proof

- Whole suite green: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` → 3726 pass, 0 fail (unshallowed first, so the two history-walking tests actually run).
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` → the same 187 advisories as `main` (file-placement, design-doc-status-banner, generated-merge-driver, rules-line-length), none from this change.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` → silent.
- The new rejection test was watched red against a mutated guard before it went green.
- No `retire:#1732` marker remains anywhere in the tree.

`missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite`, `missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite`, `missingbulb/Shepherd`
(from #2024), then `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary`, `missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite`,
`missingbulb/EdFringeNow`, `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`, `missingbulb/NoRFinder`,
`missingbulb/Shepherd` (from #2089), then `missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite`,
`missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite` again (from #2117).

## Promoted (12, from 5 of the members read)

- **basics** — fold a disclosure-copy ordering clause into the existing "changing what the software does with a user's data" rule: lead the rewritten disclosure with what is now actually done, then the narrower true claims still standing, never a blanket denial the new behavior has already made false. *(MissingBulbWebsite — the Cloudflare Web Analytics / `privacy.html` incident.)*
- **claudinite-lifecycle** — new rule: verifying "will the Stop hook block me" before committing needs `check_the_work.mjs`, never `check_the_world.mjs` — they share no code and cover disjoint rule scopes (`check_the_world`: `scope !== 'work'`, CI-wired; Stop hook: `check_the_work`'s `scope: 'work'`). *(MissingBulbWebsite — issue #208.)*
- **git-github-advanced** — six new entries:
  - Don't cite an issue/PR number before that object exists — numbers share one counter per repo and a premature citation can land on the wrong one, with no reliable comment edit path to fix it. *(Generalized from MissingBulbWebsite's "not-yet-filed issue" lesson and Shepherd's "cross-referencing an object you're about to create" lesson — independently rediscovered in two different members, a strong portability signal.)*
  - `merge_pull_request` right after a force-push to its head can 500 — the mergeable-state recompute lags the push; retry with backoff rather than reading it as a real failure. *(MissingBulbWebsite.)*
  - The tool-result cap catches a single large text result too, not only a list — `get_job_logs`'s `tail_lines` can overflow on its own, guessing a large value to pull CI context. *(Independently confirmed in EdFringeNow and GoogleCalendarEventCreator — a strong portability signal.)*
  - An overflowed `search_issues`/`search_code` result read back from its saved file is always GitHub's own `{total_count, incomplete_results, items}` envelope — index `['items']` on first parse. *(Shepherd.)*
  - New check `branch-from-bare-main` (plus its fixture, `packs/git-github/test/pack.test.mjs`) — a sandboxed checkout's local `main` can sit pinned stale, so branching from it by bare name rather than `origin/main` silently starts from frozen history. *(Shepherd's own `branch-from-local-main` local check, generalized and tightened to stop matching `git branch -d main`.)*
  - The session's own permission classifier can deny `git push --force-with-lease` outright as a destructive rewrite of an already-pushed commit, even for the smallest edit (a trailer, arming auto-merge) — add a new commit (`--allow-empty` if nothing changed) and push it as a plain fast-forward instead of amending. *(MissingBulbWebsite.)*
- **headless-browser** — a plain HTTP client can often reach a CDN from a restricted CI/sandbox environment that denies the browser's own connection to the same host; when a case needs the library's real behaviour, not just its surface stubbed, vendor the real asset via that client and route-intercept the CDN URL. *(EdFringeNow — the Leaflet/`unpkg.com` incident.)*
- **claudinite-fleet-sheepdog** — when reporting or judging what canon currently declares, read canon's own live `packs/<id>/`, never this repo's own vendored mount, which only answers what this enforcer itself runs. *(Shepherd — issue #556.)*
- **research-project** — choosing test images for a new detection/invariance harness: default to real images already at hand over a synthetic field, synthesizing only once real options are exhausted. *(NoRFinder.)*
- **cloudflare-site** — new prose rule: Workers static assets 307s a `.html` path to its extensionless form, so an internal link still naming the `.html` file costs every visitor that redirect. *(MissingBulbWebsite had already written this as a local-pack check. A canon check generalized off the wrangler config's `assets.directory` was drafted and tested in this session, but authoring a brand-new blocking check trips `consumer-safe-change` — its only additive discharge is a rehearsal fixture in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`, outside the promote stage's write surface (`promote-scope` is blocking on this branch prefix, confirmed by a red CI run when the fixture touch was included). A migration record would be the wrong tool for a purely additive check, so per `growth-promote/task.md`'s own fallback this lands as prose, with the drafted check and its test carried on a tagged conformance-backlog issue, #2129, for a session with full corpus access to land later.)*

## Rejected / not promoted

- **ClaudiniteWebsite contributed nothing new across any of the three occurrences** — every candidate was already covered:
  - "fix belongs in canon but can't be pushed from here" → already in git-github-advanced's "Write access scoped to one repo doesn't license routing around it".
  - "never also commit a canon-bound fix as this repo's own local-pack skill" → a narrow corollary of that same rule, not worth a second entry.
  - "never amend a subagent's pushed commit" / "don't shadow a dispatched subagent's read" / "search issues too after a worker-restart" → all three already in `claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md`.
  - "never `Closes #N` on a queue item's own delivered PR" → already stated in this repo's own local pack.
  - "`converge-item.mjs` step 6 fails from an MCP-only session" → **stale**: the current `packs/claudinite-tasks/public/instructions.md` already redesigned `converge-item.mjs` to never touch GitHub itself.
  - Its two declared checks (`no-server-behind-the-page`, `release-contract-carries-its-description`) are Cloudflare-specific and don't generalize; the underlying principles are already the basics privacy-disclosure and doc-claim rules.
  - Its `node-test-discovery` check duplicates the canon's already-shipped `node` pack world-rule (`test-discovery-resolves`, landed 60903.1) — same signature, same fix, same origin lesson.
  - Editing a product-wiki `## Key insights` header needing `check_the_world.mjs` run locally → already the existing claudinite-lifecycle "pushing a change that touches workflows/checks/pack config" rule, applied to one check id.
- **Shepherd**: most items are Claudinite/fleet-machinery specific and already covered (subagent scratchpad collisions, subagent-progress-after-worker-restart, "retiring a system — audit the live generator moved" — several near-verbatim). "Reading fleet activity to rank or report it, filtering Claudinite's own artifacts" was left local: `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`'s own routing guidance routes "the fleet brief" to `claudinite-dashboard`, which has no RULES.md yet. **Versions are not bumped here.** The issue asks for both packs bumped with their `VERSIONS.md` rows; this repo's standing rule is that a shared canon pack's version and its row are the canon's own tasks' to write after the change lands, never the change's (`claudinite-growth/RULES.md`). `pack-version-bump` runs on merge to main and `pack-version-history` fills the row, so both arrive by the route that keeps them correct.

**A missing target is fatal, not silent.** For a member whose executor genuinely predates #1695 this is a park, not a self-heal: the update task is what would have delivered the newer executor. That is deliberate and it is what the issue asked for — a stale mount that cannot converge itself should be visible, and the failure names the remedy (re-baseline against the canon).

## Why the diff is wider than the brief predicted

The brief predicted `packs/claudinite-tasks` and `packs/claudinite-lifecycle`; the merge policy correctly reports `AUTOMERGE: no` on two files outside them, so this PR waits for a person.

A **migration record** would have nothing to write — no member's tracked file spells these names; the tolerance's holder was the member's vendored executor, which the nightly converge already replaced. ## The premise, measured

An entry point's catch that calls `process.exit(1)` after printing discards whatever stdout has not drained. Node's stdout is synchronous for files and for pipes on Linux, so this does **not** show up in a small test — the 64 KB pipe buffer absorbs everything. It appears as soon as the reader applies backpressure:

| exit path | lines delivered | status |
|---|---|---|
| `process.exit(1)` | 309 of 200,000 | 1 |
| `process.exitCode = 1` | 200,000 of 200,000 | 1 |

Same exit status, all of the output. That is the whole change.

## Why it is safe here

All 27 sites are entry-point guards under `import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href`, and none waits on the event loop after the catch — so letting the process end naturally is equivalent to forcing it, minus the truncation.

Since #1695 the executor resolves which branch and pull request a run works on and hands it to code-work as `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_*`. Two lanes kept a decision site of their own for the window in which a member's vendored executor predated that hand-off. The window has passed, so both are gone and an absent target fails the run naming the stale executor.

(No closing keyword: #1698 is this run's own work item, and `converge-item.mjs` sets its terminal state — a native `Closes` would fire on merge and override the park.)

## What changed

- **`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs`** — no longer disposes of an incumbent found by branch prefix, and no longer mints `claudinite/update-<day>-<seed>`; `updateBranchName` is deleted. A converge with no `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_BRANCH` prints a `claudinite-needs-human: action` marker and throws. A **rehearsal is exempt**: it restores the tree and delivers nothing, and `canary-rehearsal.yml` drives this worker with no executor at all — a guard that fired there would fail the release gate on every merge to main.
- **`packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-generated.mjs`** — `branch` is required and the `branchPrefix`/`stamp` discovery is gone. Both callers (`usage-fold`, `pack-version-history`) hand in the executor's target and nothing else.
- **`packs/claudinite-tasks/land-pr.mjs`** — `openDeliveredPull` and `disposeOpenPull` deleted with their tests; `pullDisposition` stays, since the executor's target resolution judges with it.

No `retire:#1698` marker remains.

## The reading I took on two points

**Versions are not bumped here.** The issue asks for both packs bumped with their `VERSIONS.md` rows; this repo's standing rule is that a shared canon pack's version and its row are the canon's own tasks' to write after the change lands, never the change's (`claudinite-growth/RULES.md`). `pack-version-bump` runs on merge to main and `pack-version-history` fills the row, so both arrive by the route that keeps them correct.

**A missing target is fatal, not silent.** For a member whose executor genuinely predates #1695 this is a park, not a self-heal: the update task is what would have delivered the newer executor. That is deliberate and it is what the issue asked for — a stale mount that cannot converge itself should be visible, and the failure names the remedy (re-baseline against the canon).

## Why the diff is wider than the brief predicted

The brief predicted `packs/claudinite-tasks` and `packs/claudinite-lifecycle`; the merge policy correctly reports `AUTOMERGE: no` on two files outside them, so this PR waits for a person.

- `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/tasks/pack-version-history/worker.mjs` — the second caller of `deliverGenerated`. A required parameter reaches every caller, and the abstraction that would have kept the diff in one place does not exist: the two callers each read `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_BRANCH` out of the environment themselves. A `targetFromEnv()` helper in the delivery seam would collapse both call sites to one line, and is worth doing if the reviewer wants it — it is a separate change.
- `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` — the `consumer-safe-change` discharge, below.

## Which discharge, and why the fixture

`consumer-safe-change` fires on the removed exports: a member's own local pack imports the mount by name, and a dropped name throws at link time, fails that pack's load and makes the converge refuse the tree.

No previous fixture imports anything out of `.claudinite/shared/`, which is why the whole #1848 surface converged green whatever the canon did to it.

It bites: renaming `deliverGenerated` in the canon turns that fixture red in both modes (`fresh` and `stale`) and nothing else.

**The integer version spelling is declared by the canon itself (#1912).** Nineteen live migration records carry `version: 1`…`version: 6`, and `recordVersion` reads that field through `versionFromLiteral`. input.body:
Original-issue: #2084
In-production-when: `.claudinite/local/usage-review.GENERATED.json` on `main` carries a `generated` date of 2026-10-06 or later — that is the first review at which a finding standing since 2026-09-22 has reached `LASTING_DAYS`.
Verify: read that file and the repo's issues labelled `usage-finding`. Pass = the two agree in both directions. (a) Every finding in the file with `lasting: true` and `cause` of `known` or `probable` has an OPEN issue titled `Usage: <rule> - <subject>`. (b) Every OPEN issue whose title starts `Usage: ` names a subject/rule pair the file still carries; one that does not should have been closed. Fail on either mismatch, naming the finding or issue that is out of step.
Not-before: 2026-10-06T07:00:00Z
Retry-every: 7 days
Model: sonnet

The usage review's loop merged in #2214. Its first production run ([#2237](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2237), 2026-09-22) proved the half that could be watched at once: the scheduled task ran, computed 54 findings over the 28 days to 2026-09-21, opened its pull request and auto-merged it.

What that run could not prove is the filing half. `issues.mjs` files an issue only for a finding that is **lasting** (14 days) and whose cause is `known` or `probable`; on a first run every finding is dated that day, so nothing was eligible and nothing was filed. That is the gate working, not a gap — but it means the code path that asks a person for attention, and the one that closes an issue when its finding clears, have never executed.

Today's run carries exactly one `probable` finding — `check-never-fires-with-prose-twin` on `scheduler-workflows-are-thin` — so the earliest review that can file is the one whose window reaches 2026-10-06. The other 53 are `unknown` and by design never file.

The assertion is deliberately two-directional. A one-way check ("an issue exists") would pass vacuously if the finding simply cleared, and the closing path is the half with no other witness.

{"number":2084,"title":"Design the usage review: the corpus's standing feedback loop","body":"## What this is

`docs/usage-review/DESIGN.md` — the end state of a **measure → judge → act → verify** loop over what the corpus actually does in sessions: which skills load and by what cause, which checks fire, which advisories are ignored, which guards hold calls, how long the Stop hook's checks take.

- **Measure**: `usage-fold` gains counters for load cause, trigger fires and follow-through, tool calls, guard fires, advisory persistence, loop-guard relents and check timing; the runners print one machine timing line.
- **Judge**: a new weekly agentless `usage-review` task in `claudinite-growth` evaluates a fixed table of classes (S1–S6 for skills, C1–C7 and G1 for checks and guards) over the trailing four ISO weeks against the four before, with session and run floors, and lands `.claudinite/local/usage-review.GENERATED.json` on an accumulating auto-merged PR.
- **Act**: `growth-extract` consumes local findings; a new `canon-usage-review` in `claudinite-canon-curation` applies canon adaptations and runs the prose-removal experiment for never-firing checks with a prose twin; Shepherd aggregates fleet-wide.
- **Verify**: a `Rule effectiveness` retrospective per experiment; the element's own retrospective brief is in §8.

Design only — no code in this PR. The plan (steps, dependency graph, automerge policy per link) goes to the owner for approval before its tracking issue is filed.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/production-retrospective

# Production retrospective

[verify-in-production](../verify-in-production/SKILL.md) proves a **point assertion**, once:
artifact X reads Y, pass or fail. An element big enough to have a design deserves a second look of
a different kind — not "did it go live" but "did the design survive contact". Once it has worked
*as planned* for about a week, somebody should read its production record and answer four
questions:

1. **Is it working?** Every part of its loop ran and closed — count the strands, the wrong
   closes, the parks, not just the happy paths.
2. **Is it misused?** Do people or neighbouring machinery interact with it against its contract?
3. **Is it overused?** Which uses cost runs or attention and returned nothing — and what should
   the bar exclude?
4. **Is it underused?** What did the design mean to cover that nothing reaches — a trigger that
   never fires, a manual ask that should have been a mechanism?

The four questions are only the frame. What gives them teeth is a brief that already knows what
the element was *supposed* to do — and that knowledge exists exactly once, while the element is
being designed. So this skill has two moments: the brief is **written with the design**, and the
review **runs** a week into production. The reader at either moment must not be the author's
memory: the review is filed as a mechanism that comes back on its own (RULES.md's *When verifying
now is genuinely impossible* names the principle; this skill is its review-shaped sibling).

## When one is owed

The bar: **the element earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue.** A minor feature files no
retrospective — its proof is a test that ran, or verify-in-production's point assertion, and this
skill adds nothing to that. Filing retrospectives for small changes buries the reviews that matter
under reviews with nothing to find.

Two triggers own the filing today:

- **A migration plan's chain.** The retrospective is the chain's **last link**, filed with the
  rest of the chain when the plan is agreed —
  [writing-migration-plans](../writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) owns the chain's mechanics. It
  rides `Blocked-by:` on the final execution step, so the queue holds it until the migration is
  actually done.
- **A merge that completes a design-doc'd element outside any chain.** File it at the merge,
  beside verify-in-production's own filing moment — the two are separate calls, and a point
  assertion neither requires nor replaces the retrospective.

## The brief is written at design time, not when the retrospective runs

What to retrospect on is a design question, answered while the element is being designed — in the
same pass that writes the design doc, and recorded in the retrospective issue's body (with the
expectations themselves in the design doc, where they are part of the end state). Answered when
the retrospective runs it is too late twice over: the designer's intent has left everyone's head,
and a number nobody thought to record cannot be read back. The brief answers, concretely, for
*this* element:

- **What is expected to happen, and in what amounts.** Volumes and rates, not adjectives: how
  many filings, runs, adoptions, visits per week; which counts should be zero and which would be
  worrying at zero. An expectation without a quantity cannot be missed.
- **What behaviours are expected** — from users and from neighbouring machinery. Who reaches for
  it, when, instead of what; what they were doing before it existed.
- **How each expectation is measured.** The concrete artifact each number is read from — an issue
  count under a label, a run log, a usage file, a stamp, a dashboard — not "we'll see".
- **What would signal misuse** — the interactions its contract forbids, stated so a run can
  recognize them in the record.
- **What would signal overuse** — the cost that would show the bar is too low: filings that find
  nothing, runs that burn sessions to no verdict.
- **What would signal a wrong design decision.** Per decision the design doc records with its
  alternatives: what observation would mean the rejected alternative was right after all.
- **Which decisions are cheap to re-examine.** A default, a cadence, a threshold, a model choice
  can be revisited from evidence; a storage shape or a public contract cannot. Mark the cheap
  ones so the review re-opens them freely and treats the load-bearing ones as expensive claims.
- **Which metrics the review requires, and how the run will access them.** Every measurement
  above must be readable by the unattended run — name the artifact and the read. A metric that
  does not exist yet is an implementation requirement discovered at design time: build the
  counter, the log line, the label with the element itself, or the retrospective arrives with
  nothing to read (the same discipline as RULES.md's *Writing code that can silently do nothing*).

## What you file

One issue on the ad-hoc lane — the same lane and the same first-lines field-block placement
[`/do-later`](../do-later/SKILL.md) files under, with the mark it applies: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**.
Title `Retrospective: <the element, in a few words>`. Make it a **sub-issue** of the element's
tracking issue (or, with no tracker, of the design's own issue), so the element shows the review
still owed on it.

```
Blocked-by: #<the chain's final execution link>   (chain case)
Not-before: <ISO instant ≈ a week past the merge>  (merge case)
Retry-every: 7 days
Model: opus
```

`Model: opus` because this is judgment work — weighing a record against a design — not the field
read a verification makes. Never `Automerge:` — a retrospective has nothing to merge.

The body is the run's whole brief — the design-time answers above, addressed to a run that will
never see the conversation: the subject (the design doc, the tracking issue), the **record to
read** with each metric's access spelled out, the expected amounts, and the named signals for
misuse, overuse and each re-examinable decision. Then the playbook:

1. **Read when the subject completed** — the final link's close, or the merge — from the artifact
   itself, never inferred from elapsed time. The horizon runs from that instant, not from the
   filing: a chain files its retrospective at plan time, when nobody knows when the migration will
   end. Less than the horizon ago → re-arm exactly as a verification does (`Not-before:` to
   completion + horizon, clear the `task:status:*` label, no comment) and leave the issue open.
2. **Ripe → review.** Re-read what the design *promises* — the brief's expectations and signals,
   and the design doc behind them — **before reading the record**, then diff the record against it
   — RULES.md's *Correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source*, applied to
   behaviour. Answer the four questions with the brief's own measurements: counts and links, not
   impressions.
3. **Findings become issues — one issue per systemic fault, and the run fixes nothing — routed by
   kind.** An **implementation fault** — the element does not do what the design says — is a bug:
   file it as an actionable task issue the queue can implement. A **design fault** — the element
   does what the design says and the record shows that decision was wrong — is nobody's to fix
   silently: file it as a **discussion issue** carrying the evidence and the design doc's own
   alternatives, parked so it waits on the **owner's decision** (the park lever the repo's queue
   provides, or a plain ask to the owner where it has none). Comment the summary on this issue
   linking each finding, and close it as completed. Four clean answers are also a result: close
   with the summary saying so.
4. **A record the run cannot read** — an artifact behind a scope or egress wall — **parks for a
   human naming exactly which read failed.** A blocked read answers "all clean" exactly the way a
   healthy mechanism does; never convert one into a verdict.

## The lane is open: defining another retrospective class

The design retrospective above is one **class** of a general shape. A class is four things: a
**trigger** (the event that files it — an event, never a habit), a **subject and its record** (what
to read), a **horizon** (how long the subject must live before judging), and a **brief** (the
questions, usually these four re-aimed). Anyone may define another, at the scope that owns the
recurring moment:

- **A canon pack** whose territory has its own "lived long enough to judge" moment declares a
  class in its own prose or skills, routed through the growth lifecycle like any promotion.
- **A repo's local pack** defines classes for subjects only that repo has.
- **The fleet enforcer** files fleet-wide ones, where the subject spans members.

Classes worth proposing when their trigger next fires — each a proposal to its owning pack, not a
rule this skill sets:

| Class | Trigger | The brief asks |
|---|---|---|
| Post-adoption | a repo adopts Claudinite or a pack | did its tasks run, did checks stay green, did the owner fight it |
| New scheduled task | a new task's first week of runs | is the cadence right, do runs converge, is it filing noise |
| Fleet rollout | a fleet-baseline force, or a pack seeded across members | did every member converge, what parked, what stayed `unknown` |
| Rule effectiveness | a growth-extract batch lands | did the friction recur, are the rules loaded but ignored |
| Grant of a credential or permission | a token created or widened | is it used at all, is it still least-privilege |
| Retirement | a mechanism removed or a repo handed off | do references dangle, did anything break silently |

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and the horizon.

content.content:
## 9. Failure modes, stated

- A window under a floor evaluates nothing and says so; *no findings* is a result only when
  `notEvaluated` is empty.
- A counter absent from frozen weeks leaves its rules *not recorded* until enough weeks carry it.
- A capture-only repo gets no digests and says so; the rules still run from the fold.
- A false prose twin recommends an experiment on prose the check does not cover; the
  recommendation says how the experiment is read, and a reader who runs it learns so within a
  window.
- A finding issue whose review stops running stays open with a stale body; the issue names the
  review date it was last confirmed on, so staleness is readable.
- A rule whose signature nothing in the record produces never fires; the retrospective reads
  the per-rule firing history and names it.
- A triage PR left open for weeks holds its subject against a second proposal (the precondition
  excludes a subject with an open PR); a finding that worsens meanwhile shows it on the dashboard
  and in the issue, and the stale PR is closed rather than amended.
- A triage PR merged long after it was written lands a change against figures that have since
  moved; its body carries the window it was written from, and the next review re-judges the
  element on the record as it now is.

## 10. Retrospective brief

Owed once the review has landed in this repository and lived four weeks.

- **Volume.** `sessions ≥ 10` per window here; two to eight findings per review with the floors
  met (zero across two windows means the thresholds are loose, more than twelve means tight);
  read from the review file's history on `main`.
- **Every rule fires at least once in the first two months**, read off the file's history; a
  rule that never fires is re-examined before it is trusted.
- **Issues.** Between one and five `usage-finding` issues open at a time; each closed by the
  review or by a person within a month; read from the label.
- **Acted on.** At least one triage PR merged in the first two months; zero merged out of
  several opened means the recommendations are not worth acting on and the rules are revisited,
  zero opened means the gate is too tight.
- **Expectations declared.** Every canon skill carries a `usage` block within a month (the
  `unstated` list empties); read from the review file.
- **Triage.** One PR per subject and never two open at once; each PR body names the cause
  settled and the provenance fields read; a proposal the owner closes unmerged gets a
  `_declined.md` entry naming the rule, so the next triage does not re-propose it; expected
  one to three proposals a month here, read from PRs titled `Claudinite canon: usage triage`.
- **Provenance.** Entries landed from this loop equal triage PRs **merged**, never more — zero
  on a declined proposal, zero on an element the review only observed; each names its usage rule
  and its finding's issue in `Source`; read by grepping `provenance/` for `usage review rule`.
- **Underuse.** A `known`-cause finding older than 60 days with no citing change; expected zero.
- **Overuse.** Review PRs moving daily with no finding change (a stamp leak); agent-free by
  construction, so no session cost to watch. And the review PR itself left unmerged for weeks —
  it accumulates rather than superseding, so a stale one costs nothing but says the findings are
  going unread.
- **Cost.** The Stop hook's median `stopMs` rises by no more than the timing line's own cost,
  under 5 ms, read from `checkTiming` across the runner change.
- **Cheap to re-examine:** every threshold and floor, the cause of any rule, the window, the
  sample size, the twin definition, the 14-day issue threshold. **Expensive:** the counter
  shapes in the fold header, the `usage` frontmatter vocabulary, the timing line's format. Nothing
  here is expensive to *undo*: no stage of the loop leaves a record behind unless the owner merged
  the change that record describes.

input.body:
Not-before: 2026-10-20T07:00:00Z
Retry-every: 7 days
Model: opus

The usage review — the measure → judge → act loop over what the corpus does in sessions — merged on 2026-09-22 in [#2214](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2214). Its brief was written at design time in `docs/usage-review/DESIGN.md` §10 and is reproduced below, because that doc is due for deletion (#2239) and the brief must outlive it.

**Horizon: four weeks of production.** Read the merge instant from `main`'s history, not from this issue's age; if less than four weeks have passed, re-arm `Not-before:` to merge + 4 weeks, clear the `task:status:*` label, leave this open, and comment nothing.

## The subject

- The review: `packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-review/`, weekly, delivering `.claudinite/local/usage-review.GENERATED.json` on an accumulating auto-merged PR.
- The triage: `packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-triage/`, which turns a lasting finding into a proposed diff the owner merges or declines.
- The counters: `packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/`, format version 4.
- The rules: `packs/claudinite-growth/usage-rules.json`, 16 of them.

First production run: [#2237](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2237), 54 findings over the 28 days to 2026-09-21 — already above the brief's "more than twelve means tight" line on its first sighting, which is the first thing to judge.

## What to read, and the expected amounts

| Expectation | Amount | Read from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Volume | `sessions >= 10` per window; 2–8 findings per review with floors met. Zero across two windows = thresholds loose; >12 = tight | the review file's history on `main` |
| Rule coverage | every rule fires at least once in the first two months | the file's history |
| Issues | 1–5 `usage-finding` issues open at a time; each closed by the review or a person within a month | the `usage-finding` label |
| Acted on | at least one triage PR merged in the first two months. Zero merged of several opened = recommendations not worth acting on; zero opened = gate too tight | PRs titled `Claudinite canon: usage triage` |
| Expectations declared | every canon skill carries a `usage` block; the `unstated` list stays empty | the review file |
| Triage discipline | one PR per subject, never two open at once; each body names the cause settled and the provenance fields read; a declined proposal gets a `_declined.md` entry naming the rule. 1–3 proposals a month | the triage PRs |
| Provenance | entries landed from this loop **equal triage PRs merged**, never more — zero on a declined proposal, zero on an element only observed; each names its rule and its finding's issue in `Source` | `grep -r "usage review rule" packs/*/provenance/` |
| Underuse | a `known`-cause finding older than 60 days with no citing change — expected **zero** | the review file + the label |
| Overuse | review PRs moving daily with no finding change (a stamp leak); the review PR left unmerged for weeks — it accumulates rather than superseding, so a stale one costs nothing but says the findings go unread | the PR's commit history |
| Cost | the Stop hook's median `stopMs` rises by no more than the timing line's own cost, **under 5 ms** | `checkTiming` across the runner change |

## Signals

- **Misuse** — a triage PR amended rather than closed when its subject's finding worsened; a `Usage:` issue closed by hand without the finding clearing; the review's file edited by anything but the review.
- **Overuse** — findings filed that nobody acts on for two months; the `check-never-fires` class dominating every review (it was 51 of 54 on day one, so watch whether that is signal or the definition being too broad).
- **A wrong design decision** — per §8's rejected alternatives. Most sharply: the loop deliberately has **no declared rate** for a skill, only a declared *mechanism* (`adoption` | `triggered` | `judgment`). If the record shows `judgment` skills are indistinguishable from each other and no rule can ever say anything about them, the rejected "declared RATE" alternative deserves re-reading. Note the brief above predates that correction — it was written when a skill declared `loads-per-sessions`, and the rule dividing by it (`skill-routine-under-rate`) was retired with it.

## Cheap vs expensive to re-examine

**Cheap** (re-open freely from evidence): every threshold and floor, any rule's `cause`, the window, the sample size, the prose-twin definition, the 14-day issue threshold, the review's cadence.

**Expensive** (treat as load-bearing claims): the counter shapes in the fold header, the `usage` frontmatter vocabulary, the timing line's format.

Nothing here is expensive to *undo*: no stage of the loop leaves a record behind unless the owner merged the change that record describes.

## Playbook

1. Check the horizon from the merge instant. Not ripe → re-arm as above.
2. Re-read what the design promises — this brief, and `packs/claudinite-growth/README.md` — **before** reading the record. Then diff the record against it.
3. Answer the four questions with counts and links, not impressions: is it working, misused, overused, underused.
4. Findings become issues, one per systemic fault, and **this run fixes nothing**. An implementation fault (the loop does not do what the design says) is a bug — file it as an actionable task issue. A design fault (it does what the design says and the record shows the decision was wrong) is the owner's — file it as a discussion issue carrying the evidence and §8's alternatives, parked on the owner's decision.
5. Comment the summary here linking each finding, and close as completed. Four clean answers are also a result — close saying so.
6. A record you cannot read (a scope or egress wall) **parks for a human naming exactly which read failed**. A blocked read looks identical to "all clean"; never convert one into a verdict.

Merged, and the loop has now run in production.

**The merge.** `main` had moved under the branch, so it rebased rather than merged (`merge-main-into-branch` blocks the merge commit). Both conflicts were append-only provenance files — `main` had backfilled their real history while the branch carried shallow-clone placeholder `born` entries, so main's history stands and my entries append after it. Re-verified on the new base: suite 3749/3749, both sweeps 0 blocking. One warning was mine: `design-doc-status-banner` refused the design doc because *"built, not yet proven in production"* invented a third status where the vocabulary has two. The doc is in flight until a run proves it, so it says that now.

Squashed as `adb3dc8` after CI went green; conversation captured.

**Then I forced the run rather than filing a wait for it.** Scheduler dispatch with `wake=claudinite-growth/usage-review` → [run 35694909914](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/35694909914) → drain → [executor 35695006911](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/35695006911), 10 minutes, success. It ran as code-work with no agent, and it did the thing that no test could show:

> **[#2237](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2237) — "Usage review: 54 findings in the 28 days to 2026-09-21"**, opened by the task and auto-merged as `bd7da3d9`.

54 findings against 38 skills, 96 checks and 32 guards. One `probable` — `check-never-fires-with-prose-twin` on `scheduler-workflows-are-thin` — and 53 `unknown`, of which 51 are `check-never-fires`. That is already past the design's own *"more than twelve means tight"* line on first sighting, which is the first thing the retrospective should weigh.

**It filed no issues, and that is the gate working.** `issues.mjs` files only for a finding that has lasted 14 days *and* has a known or probable cause; every finding is dated today. So the filing and closing paths have still never executed — the one genuinely unwatchable part.

**Folders touched** (non-test, ignoring READMEs and history rows):

| folder | what changed |
| --- | --- |
| `docs/usage-review/` | the status banner moved to the accepted `in flight` |
| `packs/claudinite-tasks/provenance/` | two files reconciled against main's backfill |

**Filed, all on the ad-hoc queue:**

- [#2239](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2239) — delete the design doc once the loop is proven. It exists because the verification needed a real issue to reopen on failure: `#2084` is a *pull request*, so it can be neither a parent nor a landing place.
- [#2238](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2238) — the verification, sub-issue of #2239, `Not-before: 2026-10-06`, retry weekly. Its assertion is two-directional on purpose: every lasting known/probable finding has an open `Usage:` issue, **and** every open `Usage:` issue names a finding the file still carries. A one-way check would pass vacuously if the finding simply cleared, and the closing path has no other witness.
- [#2240](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2240) — the four-week retrospective, sub-issue of #2239, `Not-before: 2026-10-20`, `Model: opus`. It carries §10's brief in full, because the doc holding it is due for deletion. I noted there that the brief predates your correction — it was written when a skill declared a rate — and that the sharpest design signal to watch is whether `judgment` skills turn out indistinguishable, which is the case for re-reading the rejected rate alternative.

One thing I'd flag: I dispatched the scheduler, which is a live effect on the repo, without asking first. The standing rule for changed unattended machinery is to force a run now rather than wait, and the dispatch only wakes an already-declared task, but it did open and auto-merge a PR — worth knowing I took that as covered rather than as needing its own approval.

> ⚠️ Still open: [#2238](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2238) (verification, 2026-10-06), [#2240](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2240) (retrospective, 2026-10-20) and [#2239](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2239) (delete the design doc, blocked on the verification). All three come back on their own; no polling armed, per your standing rule.

import json,glob,re,subprocess
tracked=subprocess.run(['git','ls-files'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.split('\n')
ids=set("""claude-md-length declared-check-since declared-check-spec-keys improve-comments-scope no-conflict-markers shared-constants warning-suppression work-request-not-started preferences-provenance preferences-store-configured preferences-store-file-names author-association-as-permission engine-release-record fixture-git-housekeeping home-seeded-packs-declared hook-judges-never-exit scheduler-workflows-are-thin year-last-digit-rollover pack-directory-kebab-case pack-discovery-entry-await pack-no-enforcement-narration pack-version-log-ordered skill-usage-declared dedup-prune-integrity growth-write-scope in-session-github-access legacy-check-spellings routine-structure task-declaration-matches-folder task-md-only-when-agentic task-worker-restores-main technology-skill-cites-dated-sources technology-skill-code-imports-inside-its-folder technology-skill-links-inside-its-folder adoption-answers-pending claudinite-lifecycle-declared conformance-work-scope conformance-workflow interview-answer-stale legacy-shape-in-use scheduler-workflow-shape seeded-file-stale""".split())
def jsre(p):
    m=re.match(r'^/(.*)/([a-z]*)$',p or '')
    if not m: return None
    try: return re.compile(m.group(1))
    except re.error: return None
rows=[]
for p in glob.glob('packs/**/declared-checks.json',recursive=True)+glob.glob('.claudinite/local/packs/**/declared-checks.json',recursive=True):

        rw=c.get('relevantWhen') or {}

        rows.append((c['id'],c.get('severity'),json.dumps(rw) if rw else '-',n))
for r in sorted(rows):
    print(f"{r[0]:48} {str(r[1]):9} scope={str(r[3]):5} relevantWhen={r[2][:70]}")

content.text:
I checked all 51. You're right, and the problem is worse than the adoption case — **fewer than half could have fired at all.**

## What the 51 actually are

| class | n | evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Born inside the window** | 13 | `since` dates from 2026-09-03 to 2026-09-21. `fixture-git-housekeeping` and `skill-usage-declared` landed on the window's last day |
| **Structurally inert in the canon** | 12 | 6 gated on `.claudinite/shared`, which this repo does not have; 2 on the adoption interview; 3 on a preferences store this repo isn't; 1 on `seedOps` |
| **Dead scope — matches nothing** | 1 | `in-session-github-access` scans `^(routines\|migrations)/`; the tree has **0** such files |
| **Tiny scope** | 9 | every `gha/*` check scans `.github/workflows/` — **5 files**, all thin wrappers the repo's own rules keep minimal |
| Residue, genuinely preventive | 16 | `no-conflict-markers` (2267 files), `warning-suppression` (912), etc. Zero here is the check working |

`fixture-git-housekeeping` is the sharpest case: the review says it never fires, and it threw **13 advisories** in the sweep I ran an hour ago. It was one day old.

Your adoption point generalizes past skills. For a legacy-tolerance advisory, an adoption-time check and a member-conformance check, **zero is the designed outcome** — the rule treats the success state as suspicious.

## Three implementation faults, separate from the design question

1. **`check-never-fires` double-counts.** It carries no `and` clause, so it fires for every zero-firing check *including* ones with a prose twin — while its finding text asserts "and has no prose twin". `scheduler-workflows-are-thin` appears twice in one report, under both rules.
2. **No `since` awareness.** A check younger than the window is judged on a window it didn't exist for.
3. **`in-session-github-access` is dead** and nothing says so — precisely the failure `writing-check-selects` exists to catch. That's a real bug in that check, worth its own issue whatever happens to the rules.

## On the denominator

You've named the actual defect. `runs: 2276` is **one global number, byte-identical across all 51 findings** — it counts sweeps, not opportunities for that check. A check gated on an absent path is indistinguishable from one evaluated 2276 times and finding nothing.

The good news: all four metrics you named are **already in the fold**, so this needs no new instrumentation — `userMessages`, `tokensIn`/`tokensOut`, `prs`, and `queue.done` are recorded per day and per week.

One thing I'd want your call on before building, because my investigation suggests checks and skills may not want the same denominator:

questions.question: A rule compares a count against a denominator. What should that denominator be?

options.label: Opportunity for checks, activity blend for skills
options.description: A check is normalised by how often it could have fired (files in its scope, times runs it was actually relevant for) — a structural measure. A skill is normalised by the blended activity rate you described (per user prompt / per token / per PR / per closed issue). The two element kinds genuinely measure different things: a check's silence is about its scope, a skill's is about how busy the repo was. This is what the investigation points at, but it means two mechanisms rather than one.

It would still fix the 'runs: 2276 for everything' defect, since the blend moves with real activity. But it would not by itself catch the dead check or the structurally-inert class, because those are about scope rather than activity.

# Changing a pack's elements

A pack's carriers - the rules in `RULES.md`, a skill and its triggers, a coded or declared
check, a task and its policy, the manifest - say *what* a session does. The decision behind
each - why it reads so, who decided, from what evidence, why this carrier and this trigger,
what was rejected, what would retire it - is one append-only file per element under the
pack's `provenance/`, read by maintenance and never by a session. Three things follow for
any edit under a pack.

## 1. The edit owes an entry, in the same change

Every change to what a carrier decides lands with an entry on the element's file, and the
`provenance-change-recorded` check says so again at the Stop hook when it did not. Which
file: the marker that ends a rule or guideline names it (`(url-filter-host-operators)` →
`provenance/url-filter-host-operators.md`), and two carriers may name one file while their
history is one; an unmarked guideline's is its skill's; a skill's is its directory name; a
check's its id with `/` as `-`; a task's its id; the manifest's `_pack.md`. Which kind:

| The change | Kind |
|---|---|
| a rule, guideline, skill body or step reads differently | `reworded` - or `strengthened` / `weakened` when the modality moved |
| a rule split in two, or two folded into one | `split` / `merged` (an entry on every file involved) |
| a guideline given a file of its own, its history having diverged from its skill's | `split` on the skill's file, `born` on the bullet's, with `Mechanism` |
| a rule moved to another carrier or pack | `moved`, with `Mechanism` |
| prose turned into a check | `converted`, with `Mechanism` and the deletion-test verdict |
| a skill's description or `force-load-on-*` trigger | `trigger-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a task's preconditions, `expected_outcome`, `automerge`, model or worker | `policy-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a check's severity, scope or gate | `severity-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a new element | `born`, with `Mechanism` - and `mark` first if the carrier has no file |
| an element removed | `retired` - the file stays, and this is its last entry |
| a review that found new evidence or changed the retire test | `reaffirmed`; a review that found nothing new writes nothing |

No entry is owed for whitespace, a re-wrap, a code comment in a check, a fixture, a test, a
README row, a version bump, or the marking pass's own markers and `body:` lines.

Write the entry in the file grammar and append it through the tool, which validates it and
refuses one that carries a secret:

```
node packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs append <pack> <element> <<'EOF'
## 2026-09-21 · reworded · the consequence clause said why twice (#2210)
- **Reason:** the second sentence restated the rule; cut.
- **Actor:** @handle (owner).
- **Model:** <the model this session runs, as the harness names it>
- **Landed:** #2210
EOF
```

In a member the tool is `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs`, and
the pack is under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. `--changed` in place of the element appends the
same entry to every element the working tree's diff touched - a sweep's one-line entries.
The fields, each written only where there is something behind it: `Source`, `Reason`,
`Actor` (the person by handle with their role, or the run and who merged it - never an
email), `Model`, `Mechanism` (the carrier and its trigger, and why - required on `born`,
`converted`, `moved`, `trigger-changed`, `policy-changed`, `severity-changed`), `Rejected`,
`Retire when`, `Landed`. An entry never restates the rule: the carrier is the description,
the entry is the decision. A candidate turned down goes on `_declined.md` the same way, kind
`declined`, with `Source`, `Reason` and `Actor`.

A file is meant to grow: a wrong entry is answered by a later one. The check advises against a
line lost or altered and refuses nothing; the one rewrite that is right is the backfill replacing
what the conversion wrote with the element's derived history, once.

## 2. The README carries use, never history

A pack's `README.md` is for the person adopting the pack or reaching for one of its
elements: when the pack activates, what each check demands and what satisfies it, when a
skill is the thing to load, what the task does to the repository, and the catalog of what
the pack carries. Never how an element came to be, what it replaced, why its id reads as it
does, what an earlier shape did, or how the pack is maintained. The test is the sentence: a
date, a pull request number, an "until", a "was", a "kept as it was" or a "distilled from"
is a decision, and a decision is an entry on the element's file - `_pack.md` for the pack's
own shape. Move it there; do not write it here.

## 3. The mount is never edited

A file under `.claudinite/shared/` arrived from a canon and the next converge replaces the
whole tree. Change it in the canon, or carry the difference in the repo's own
`.claudinite/local/packs/`.

## 2026-09-22 · strengthened · the rule excludes what its sibling claims (#2214)
- **Reason:** it carried no `and`, so it fired for every check with no findings including
  the ones the prose-twin rule already claimed - and said "and has no prose twin" while
  testing nothing of the sort. The first production review reported
  `scheduler-workflows-are-thin` twice, under two rules and two different causes, which is
  what a reader weighing 54 findings has to discount by hand.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude Opus 5, per the commit trailer.
- **Mechanism:** `and: "!proseTwin"`. The evaluator gained a `!` prefix on a live predicate
  rather than a second grammar: two rules reading one record half need to split the
  subjects between them, and negation is the whole of what that takes. Unknown still
  propagates - a predicate that could not be read is unread whichever way the rule asked.
- **Landed:** #2214
EOF
node packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs append claudinite-growth usage-review <<'EOF'
## 2026-09-22 · policy-changed · an adoption date is not read off the clone's depth (#2214)
- **Source:** the owner's note that a skill reached only at adoption is not strange to find
  unloaded, 2026-09-22.
- **Reason:** `packDeclaredAt` searched the settings file's history for the first commit
  naming a pack, and its own comment claimed a shallow clone answered `null`. It did not:
  the search returns the earliest commit the checkout REACHES, which is a real commit, so
  the adoption window started at the clone's horizon. The canon declared these packs long
  before any practical fetch depth, so the window read as closed and open on two checkouts
  of one repository - the same review over the same record finding different things.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude Opus 5, per the commit trailer.
- **Mechanism:** the match is trusted only when the commit BEFORE it did not already carry
  the pack; no parent plus a shallow repository is unknowable and answers null. The
  adoption rules then read *not recorded*, which is what the comment always promised.
- **Retire when:** members carry a declaration date of their own and no history walk is
  needed to find one.
- **Landed:** #2214
EOF
echo ok

git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1
A rule's floor asks how busy the repo was, not how often the sweeps ran

Three faults the first production review exposed, and the denominator the
owner asked for.

The floor read `runs` or `sessions`. `runs` is one global number the window
carries once - 2276, identical in every one of the 54 findings - so the
floor passed always and no rule was ever gated. It now reads `activity`: a
weighted blend of what the owner asked for, what the conversation cost,
what shipped and what closed, each scaled to a common unit so the weights
are the blend's only bias. One measure, a different bar per subject kind.
Over the two windows it was calibrated on the blend moves 8.4x (453 against
54) where `runs` was flat, so `checks-slower` now refuses to compare against
a window that was barely active.

`check-never-fires` carried no `and`, so it also claimed every check the
prose-twin rule claimed, while its text said "and has no prose twin". The
review reported one check twice under two causes. The evaluator gained `!`
on a live predicate - the whole of what two rules reading one record half
need to split the subjects between them.

`packDeclaredAt` promised in its own comment that a shallow clone answers
null. It did not: `git log --reverse -S` returns the earliest commit the
checkout REACHES, so the adoption window started at the clone's horizon and
one review over one record found different things on two checkouts. The
match is now trusted only when the commit before it did not already carry
the pack.

Refs #2084
